arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence.

lives_at.note: Not attested: the lists that name this person give no address. The placement sweep assigns homes once the resident list is complete (T-0514, the owner's own sequencing) and this pass will not guess one.

works_at.note: Not attested. No trade is recorded here, so there is no premises to seek; T-0633 is where a later directory's address gets back-projected.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD DOES NOT REACH THE DAY. Every source that names this person falls on one side of 1 July 1835, and nothing follows them to it or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap.

occupation.note: No source in this pass's evidence records an occupation for this person. A poll list, a tax list, a muster roll and a baptismal entry each print a name and no trade, and where a later directory prints one it is a trade of 1843 — T-0633 is the rule for back-projecting that, and this pass does not have it.

persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented once and corroborated by nothing else, so the weakest rung of `inferred` the owner's ladder defines. A SINGLE APPEARANCE AND NOTHING ELSE. Read from poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G3), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1834 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Morrison, Ordemus” (poll_1834_076, line 245). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Morrison' agrees with the entry's forenames; 5 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: The surname agrees letter for letter, d and s are one substitution apart in a worn impression, and Orsemus Morrison is one of the town's documented carpenters: the 1833 tax list, Fergus 1843 ('Morrison, Orsemus, carpenter, res 153 Clark [died Jan. 4,1864, a. 58½]') and Norris 1844 ('carpenter, house Clark st'). 'Ordemus' is a forename that exists nowhere else in the corpus, which is the profile of a mis-read rather than a man.
merge_ruling.against_merge: TWO ROLLS OF ONE TRANSCRIPTION, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'Morrison, Orsemus' is the 1833 tax list (line 128) and 'Morrison, Ordemus' the poll filed 11 August 1834 (line 245) — and that poll also enters 'Morrison, J. M.' at line 244, so the roll that set Ordemus was setting Morrisons carefully. No roll sets both forenames; a shared source id is not a shared printing. The town holds five Morrison cards, so the surname decides nothing. D9, and the forename's absence from the rest of the corpus is kept in `for_merge` because it is what a reading of the 1834 poll's image would test.
